fatal_errors: The proposed post-fabrication heat treatment does not reconstruct the target intervention of laser-assisted machining of a DED-fabricated Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni alloy.
The cited evidence only proposes serrated grain boundaries as a possible approach; it does not demonstrate that they improve yield strength and ductility in an SLM HEA.
The claimed 10–15% improvements in both ductility and yield strength are unsupported by the cited evidence.
The intervention is under-specified and potentially combines two interventions—heat treatment and minor alloying—without defining composition, temperature, duration, or cooling schedule.
Failure to form serrated boundaries would show failure of the processing protocol, not falsify the claimed causal effect of successfully formed serrated boundaries.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses elevated-temperature degradation in additively manufactured HEAs and offers a scientifically plausible grain-boundary-engineering alternative. Its untreated control, high-temperature tensile measurements, and microscopy provide a reasonable initial test. However, it disagrees with the hidden target on alloy, manufacturing route, intervention, temperature regime, mechanism, baseline comparison, and outcomes: the target concerns laser preheating during machining above roughly 800 °C, with reduced cutting force, roughness, and work hardening rather than improved service-temperature tensile strength. Evidence discipline is weak because E1 documents hot-ductility loss and mentions SEGB formation only as a proposed solution; it does not support the quantitative effect size, simultaneous strength and ductility gains, or the stated SLM-specific range. A stronger experiment would first specify a reproducible heat-treatment-only protocol, verify SEGB formation, include a heat-treated non-serrated control, and test whether the degree of serration predicts strength and elongation independently of precipitate fraction and grain size.
